doc.title: Josiah "Cie" Frazier and Alfred Williams Interview, 1961-01-18

title: Hand position and left-handed drummers
summary: Cie asks to review stick position, and they discuss the right-angle hand position and a left-handed set-up, mentioning Joe Watkins.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: Oh, no, no. I just wanted to hear the remarks you had to make. Oh, yeah, I see what you mean. I stuck that mic right up in front of you, hoping that we can hear in your voice. I think it came through pretty well. Yeah. No, there's nothing. I said I wouldn't interfere and bother you just as long as we kept down what you were talking about.

We missed the beginning. One little thing I was going to ask you about, the position of the sticks, if you don't mind. I guess it wouldn't hurt to review that about a half a minute. Yeah. Because we didn't get that when I didn't have my machine. I see, yeah. Were you showing him how any special way to hold the sticks? Does it hold the hands farther? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Or didn't you hold your left hand up? See, I was holding it like that. Well, you're powering down almost. No, no, just the position of the hand. Parallel, yeah. See, I was playing. No, you don't want to. Right angle. Yeah, that's it. So it makes a right angle more, nearly right angle. I didn't catch it. I was in the back. I couldn't hear what you were. Yeah. He always was afraid to see it.

See, he's got his position, his snags in the position. It's like a right-hand man be playing. But they say he got it to the left side. Now, if I was playing, I'd have a snag drum on this side, you see, with my right foot on the bass drum. But he's got it parallel to his left. But yet, no, I thought a left-hand drummer could have a snag drum like this.

Yeah, like Joe Watkins. Yeah. Another fellow snags in Chicago. Yeah. That's real left-hand drum playing like that. But he still don't play any of it. In that case, he's a right-handed drum player. But he didn't put it, see. Well, I understand.
So that makes him want to put the snare on.

Yeah, I'll say what you mean. It's like a right-hand drum would play. See, see, when Joe, you know Joe's left hand, you know, when he rolls into a row, from watching him, instead of rolling, I'm rolling like that, and you probably. He rolls in with this. He rolls with this one and plays this. He rolls in with this one. Yeah. I can't do it, but he starts. Yeah. He rolls with this one. Yeah. I can't do that. When you got your position, I need to take your sticks again.

Yeah. When we pack up and make that switch to you. See, like this. That's your left. Since you, you play with the left foot, but yet, no, you use the right hand. Yeah. You want the sticks like this. You see? And that's, that's my position of playing at all times. Yeah. Just like this finger here. It's gonna hit that stick. But that's, I couldn't play it if I had to do it like that. But that's the position I'm making. See, now I close my hand. These fingers are down there. Just because you've gotten it. These fingers are free. I might put them out like that. Yeah. That was the drum roll. That was a god because when the stick gets cramped me like that. Yeah. Yeah. I couldn't make it like that.
